newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korean firms freeze some wages, currency wobbly.
newsitem.headline: Korean firms freeze some wages, currency wobbly.

text.p: South Korean industrial groups, their profits savaged by falling exports, on Tuesday decided to freeze executive pay, but backed away from a tougher plan to cut jobs and hold down wages for all workers.
The Korean won remained weak after dropping to an all-time low against the dollar on Monday. It ended unchanged on Tuesday after the central bank helped prop up the currency.
A meeting of heads of 30 leading conglomerates, known as chaebol, adopted a watered-down version of an austerity plan mapped out last week by their corporate planners.
That plan envisaged a freeze on total salary spending next year combined with early retirement schemes, virtually unheard of in a country where jobs are guaranteed for life.
"They agreed today to freeze total spending on wages and benefits for executives of 30 top groups," an official of the Federation of Korean Industries told a news conference.
The freeze would take effect next year.
"Wage freezes are not just for the benefit of the companies. They are a token of our efforts to step into the ranks of advanced countries," Chun Dae-joo said.

But Chun said for workers below executive level, the chaebol will follow guidelines set out by the Korea Employers' Federation, which represents about 350 domestic companies and deals mainly with labour-management relations.
Plunging prices for South Korea's leading exports, including semiconductors, steel and petrochemical products, have slashed profits.
South Korea's trade deficit ballooned to $11.6 billion in the first seven months of 1996 against $6.5 billion a year earlier. Some economists predict the shortfall this year could reach $20 billion.
Profits of manufacturing firms on the Seoul stock exchange dropped by more than half in the first six months of the year.

Economists said the government was allowing the won to weaken in order to claw back some of the country's price competitiveness. A weak won makes exports cheaper, although it also drives up import costs and risks inflation.
Among the chaebol heads at the meeting were the chairmen of the giant Samsung and LG groups.
Chaebol dominate the South Korean economy. Combined sales of the largest four represent 84 percent of the country's gross domestic product and 60 percent of exports.

The government looks to chaebol to implement its economic policies in the private sector. Earlier this month, the finance ministry announced an austerity plan that included wage freezes for public servants and cuts in utility fees.
Chun said the issue of early retirement schemes was not raised at Tuesday's meeting.
The Federation of Korean Trade Unions had warned that any move to slash payrolls would plunge labour-management relations "into a whirlpool".
On Monday, veteran opposition leader Kim Dae-jung blamed President Kim Young-sam for what he called an economic crisis and said workers should not be made to suffer.
Analysts generally dismissed as window-dressing Tuesday's decision on executive wage freezes.

"I am sceptical about the efficiency of such a move," said Lee Hahn-koo, president of Daewoo Reserch Institute. He said South Korea needed wage cuts, not freezes, to combat twin problems of high costs and low efficiency.
Average pay has risen by 15 percent each year since 1987, driving chaebol overseas and leading to fears of a hollowing-out of local industry.
